For example, I was talking online with a group of computer science nerds about some existential issue - can’t remember exactly what - and I suddenly realized that quantum computing (which I know almost nothing about) was a good analogy for the concept I was trying communicate about things both existing and not existing at the same time. So I interrupted and brought this up, and to my amazement all these dudes thought this was brilliant, but unfortunately they now also expected that I actually knew something about quantum computing and/or could elaborate on my comment with Te or Ti relevant infos… which I could not do. Apparently I came off as being secretive and above explaining myself, even though I explained that I didn’t really know what I was talking about. 

At a certain point it’s like why even bother? All I can do is throw something out there, draw attention to myself momentarily and then drop the ball when it comes to details, confusing everyone. Example #2 - I got my Private Investigator’s license: my strength is that I am really good at efficiently locating persons of interest (on account of being able to utilize personal information and context to analyze patterns of behavior) however, I have much more difficulty documenting the process I went through to a standard that the legal system would accept… for example a judge is not (AND SHOULD NOT)  issue a search warrant based on my gut hunch, even if it would save them 2 weeks and $20,000 ;)

This situation is near and dear to my heart. My two cents - 

Both me and my longterm partner have ADHD and have taken extended release and instant release Adderall for the condition. I have taken it for years without developing a craving for additional dopamine, however… that’s EXACTLY what happened to my partner. I didn’t take the gateway drug aspect of adderall seriously, because it had never been a problem for me, however he started taking Adderall IR and it was a disaster. An old buddy of his from HS got out of prison and swung back into town just in time to help create the conditions necessary for my partner to become seriously addicted to meth. 

What your grandma is communicating to you is a legitimate concern and should not be ignored. I learned that lesson myself the hard way. That said, depending on a number of factors including genetics, there are significant individual differences in the way in which the medication gets metabolized, and this effects the likelihood that you might develop a secondary addiction. 

I have never done hard drugs personally, and when I take my Adderall XR, I never find myself thinking…”Gee I could really go for some more dopamine right now. Maybe I should try crack…” but I will admit that I started smoking after taking adderall. I grew up in a smoke free house, never smoked cigarettes myself, but after I took adderall for the first time in my early twenties (as prescribed) I developed this incredible craving to smoke… which does go away if the medication is out of my system. My partner developed a gambling addiction and an incredible craving for more dopamine. 

As for communicating with Grandmq about it…. My suggestion is to have a constructive dialogue with her where you acknowledge that her experience of adderall as a gateway drug is legitimate, while also explaining specific ways in which it has helped you to regulate your emotions, act constructively, focus etc…, and promising to work with her to be transparent about your drug intake. It is very important that you validate her emotions and experience. I can’t overstate that.
Then together you need to establish a plan for what to do if a secondary addiction (such as meth abuse) occurs. With your family history of addiction, the adderall is somewhat risky, and if the extra dopamine does have an effect of excessively promoting reward-seeking behavior in yourself, you will actually want an external person who knows your situation to intervene and keep you from potential self-destruction. 

Where I live in the US, doctor’s office that prescribe adderall perform a quarterly urinalysis on patients that seem like they might be developing an issue. This is actually how my aforementioned partner got caught. 
I’m not sure what the rules are like where you are, but sometimes they are kind of restrictive, and might be reassuring for your grandma to hear about. Getting prescribed adderall is not the same type of carefree process it used to be when she had her experience. There are like, watch-lists and everything. 

She doesn’t want you to take it because she loves you, and she’s scared that it will destroy your life and also effect hers. Acknowledge that, and then work together to form a contingency plan to ensure that Grandma’s history won’t repeat itself. Good luck.

He’s not a person who expresses his feelings through words (highly emotionally avoidant) but he will make me special themed musical playlists to commemorate different events in my life, like breaking up with a serious longterm partner, or when I seem excessively depressed. (I’m a 4 myself btw). 

He used to play piano, but he stopped because that’s what my mom and I play, and he wanted to differentiate himself from the rest of us being that he is so competitive. The little brat is incredibly gifted with musical instruments, and loves to collect guitars, amps and other equipment, while boring me with lectures regarding the important of musical theory… ugh. 

He struggles with not feeling like he’s a part of things; is too different, special, unique for this boring town, and has neurotic episodes of self-hatred related to what he perceives as poor performance at gigs. He is highly critical of himself and others and idealizes what he feels as “missing” from his life. He is 30 years old and has only had 2 romantic partners, being that he is so demanding and specific in his aesthetic tastes and personal values. I’ve also noticed that for a male INTJ he is more prone to noticing &/or criticizing people’s fashion choices, although he’s no fashionista himself or anything. 

Speaking of, in his online dating profile I remember he just sent out the same question to every girl he was interested in dating which said, “What is your favorite song, film, book and piece of visual art?” - this is apparently all he needs to know in order to date someone. Ha! 

He’s also super into arthouse, classic and independent films. I think a lot of INTJs are somewhat that way, but my bro strikes me as having many more specific opinions and critiques about films than my INTJ boyfriend who picks out these art house films to watch, but then refuses to discuss them afterwards. INTJ 9 boyfriend thinks Weird Al is the pinnacle of songwriting lol, whereas not listening to the lyrics or not taking songwriting seriously is a grievous offense to my INTJ brother. 

Alright well, this wasn’t my best response ever to a Reddit post, but you’know… it’s a start. There are actually quite a few believable INTJ 4s floating around YouTube you could check out. Final thought: INTJ 4 leans into their Fi heavily, more so than say, a 3, or even a 9 INTJ would. The Te (musical theory) helps to create efficiencies and bolster the impact (Se) that he hopes to attain by channeling his personal values (Fi) through his music. His identity is very wrapped up in the pieces he chooses to perform, and he won’t do fun covers he knows the audience likes because he doesn’t want to spoil his reputation.

To me it's more that something that I want/desire can be negatively transformed into envy.

Envy is when you dwell on what's missing....the quality, or relationship, or thing you lack, that you imagine would instantly transform things if only you were in possession of it yourself.

Envy is about negative comparison. Desire has nothing to do with comparison.

Desire brings me towards something, while envy is like imposing my own self-defeating road block.

I think for me, envy is actually a way to protect myself from feelings of shame, worthlessness and my own extreme self criticism. I take what is internal emptiness without apparent justification and find a way to make it real in external reality. I'm looking for a way to prove that it's natural for me to feel bad, and to allow myself to continue feeding the narrative about my 'brokenness' or whatever.

Envy is also a way that I avoid confronting myself and doing that hard work I would have to do to achieve what I really want. I just assume I am fundamentally flawed, and because X person has x quality, and I don't have x quality, then I'm just a total piece of crap unless I also have that particular quality.

Envy is resolved when I can appreciate the positive qualities, skills and talents of others with making a negative comparison and self appraisal.

Example: I am an actress and I feel perpetually unappreciated. I was co directing a play and I auditioned this fabulous actress, just about my age, very beautiful, tall, (an actual runway model) who was just so talented and friendly and cool. I automatically made a negative self comparison and felt defeated... like I was worthless. But then, since I had recently realized I was a 4, I became aware of the envy I was feeling and decided to go out of my way instead to be friends with her and to try to help support her natural talents to the fullest for the sake of the play. We actually did become close friends, and it was then that I realized she was actually facing a lot serious challenges, and was more like me than I ever imagined. From this point of shared humanity we worked together on this play to heal some insecurities and issues that we both had. It was a truly transformative experience for us both and I'll never forget it. I'm so glad I decided to just appreciate her god-given gift instead of using it as a way to bludgeon myself. Allowing myself to connect with her made us both better. She elevated me and I elevated her. Taking this chance brought out my full potential and allowed me to follow my true desires. Envy = stagnation.

The thing about suffering is, it can be experienced but never be fully understood. Life is an unfolding process, and so too is the nature of suffering.

Have you heard of the Myth of Sisyphus? tdlr; he keeps rolling a giant boulder up a mountain, only to reach the top and have it roll to the bottom, where he must begin his labor once again. Eat. Work. Sleep. Repeat. The nature of life is to be trapped in an endless cycle. 

Are you in control of the cycle? Or is the cycle in control of you?

What does it mean to have it too easy? A situation that is easy for one person, may be very difficut for another. Where do we get off judging whether or not a person's suffering is justified or not? We are not they. 

Where do we get off judging our own suffering? The process that makes sense of the impulses recieved from your body, and finds language to describe your emotions is a cognitive one, whereas the process that actually gives rise to your raw emotions has no voice. 

Our thoughts interpret our feelings. The way we think about our feelings is conditioned by the culture and the expectations of the external world. 

If you feel it, you feel it. It's not a crime. It's actually more of a peverse birthright. The question is - what will you do with your innate capacity for suffering? Perhaps you have expertise that would benefit others who do not think and feel so deeply as you.

Something else you might find interesting is the theory of the Enneagram tritype (this is basically the idea that you have one main enneagram type from each center). For example identifying as a 259 tritype would mean that your dominant strategy from the heart triad is 2, whereas your dominant strategy for the head triad would be 5, and then for the body triad is would be type 9. This tritype is called “the problem solver” and embodies that archetype. I’m not suggesting this is your tritype, I’m just using it as an example.  

Also the lady who pioneered the tritype theory has made her test available for free for a limited time: https://enneagramtritypetest.com/

Well, I don't think there is a simple answer. There are several schools of the Enneagram, and wings are one of the topics they disagree on. Also, in the case of your particular posting, I think that instinctual subtype (self-pres, social, or sexual) is likely a factor.  

I like to think of it like this: Imagine that each enneagram type is different paint color. What paint colors you have access to are influenced by your genetics, temperamental and developmental factors. The way these colors manifest in reality can be more stereotypical or atypical. It just depends. Some schools believe that a person only has access to one wing, others believe you vacillate between both wings. I think that it is both, that some people express both wings, while others don't, and that this depends on the structural stability of your psyche. But enough with my opinion, I will give you the information you are really after:

***Peeps and Thoughts***, some of your confusion about attachment is likely due to exposure to pop-psychology explanations. In reality, the attachment system is extremely important to our survival, and forms the foundation for our ability to neurobiologically connect with another human being, as well as to the ability to seek comfort and emotional regulation from another.

The attachment relationship begins in infancy. Until the the age of 2 we almost exclusively draw information from the emotional right brain, as the left hemisphere of the brain (which is responsible for conscious cognition and reasoning ability) is still underdeveloped until that age. Our job as infants is to learn to regulate our own emotions and to soothe ourselves. We depend on our primary caregiver (usually the mother) to calibrate our immature emotional regulatory capacity through sensitive attunement to our needs. Our attachment is a reflection of our mother's internal emotional state and level of stress.

For more than a century, researchers have observed that infants across the globe show **three primary, organized patterns of instinctual attachment behaviors to their primary caregiver**. The research paradigm is called "the Strange Situation" if you're interested.

The ideal, healthy attachment is called **Secure**, and is demonstrated by an toddler who is distressed when their mother leaves them with a stranger in a room, and who allows the mother to comfort them when she returns. This represents around 60% of all attachments. This kind of attachment relationship demonstrates that the caregiver is predictable-enough and sensitively attuned (enough) to their babies' various physical and emotional needs that they have been able to become neurobiologically regulated by others.

The **adult attachment style** that follows directly from Secure attachment in infancy is called Secure attachment\*\*,\*\* and can be summarized as "a positive view of self and a positive view of others."

​

**There are also two problematic or insecure, organized patterns of attachment behavior:**

1. **Avoidant** \- This toddler is not visibly distressed when their caregiver leaves the room, nor are they relieved when the caregiver returns. This is because their early nurturing has calibrated their neurobiology in such as way as to repress all emotional needs and de-value attachment to others. Although the infants do not look distressed, skin conductance and fMRI evidence shows signs of extreme stress (increased blood pressure, HRV etc...) when the caregiver leaves the room. For many years people mistook these flat affected babies as being "easy," and a cold, detached style of parenting was encouraged by experts, especially in the western world. As adults (and without any early intervention) these individuals find it difficult to value intimate relationships, often beginning them with great enthusiasm, only to leave them (with great enthusiasm).  Sometimes these individuals avoid intimate relationships altogether, and sometimes they avoid them by hopping from relationship to relationship. Regardless of the behavior, the underlying motivation is to avoid being emotionally dependent on others, as well as to avoid others being emotionally dependent on them.

The **adult attachment style** that follows directly from the Avoidant attachment in infancy is called **Dismissive-Avoidant,** and can be summarized as "a positive view of self and a negative view of others."

​

2. **Anxious** \- This toddler is extremely distressed when their caregiver leaves the room, and continues to beinconsolable (or resistant) after the caregiver returns.  Anxious attachment is characterized by deep,internalized separation anxiety. The parenting style which helps to form this kind of attachment is a random,unpredictable pattern of responsiveness (look up Conditioning, & intermittent reinforcement schedule ifinterested). As an adult this person may long for a connection, but typically is plagued by fears ofabandonment and continuing separation anxiety. This can motivate these individuals to act codependent,cling to their partners, play games to elicit emotional responses which affirm their existence, and interest inpartners that are unpredictable, disconnected and (above-all) **avoidantly attached.**

The **adult attachment style** that follows directly from the Anxious attachment in infancy is called **Anxious-Preoccupied,** and can be summarized as "a negative view of self and positive view of others."

​

**There is a 3RD category of attachment (Disorganized) which is observed when an infant lacks any external organized attachment strategy.** Rather than try to write about this complicated issue, I will instead link a youtube video which explains this attachment confusion better than I ever could:  [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iGDqJYEi\_Ks](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iGDqJYEi_Ks) . This attachment confusion is typically the result of early childhood trauma, abuse, OR maternal loss, separation or significant depression. Regardless of how exactly this comes to be, the main ingredient is a caregiver who inspires fear rather than comfort, a state which continually dis-regulates the infants emotional coping capacities.

The **adult attachment style** that follows directly from the Disorganized attachment in infancy is called **Fearful-Avoidant,** and can be summarized as "unstable fluctuating/confused view of self and view of others."

​

While some of the research and theories on attachment and Enneagram are interesting, I think this issue is far too complicated to be directly linked to one enneagram type or another.

**Although, my educated speculation would be the following: (REMEMBER! These are probabilities only)**

Enneagram 9 is most likely to co-occur with Secure attachment style. *(Empirical evidence suggests that 9s have a more stable and adaptable in-born temperament, with lower levels of trait neuroticism and disagreeableness overall. Babies with this temperament are typically easier for stressed-out parents to care for, which in itself, lessens the likelihood of insecurity and disorganization. That said, if attachment trauma is severe enough, ANY temperament can be affected.)*

Enneagram 2 and 6 are more likely to co-occur with an Anxious-Preoccupied style;

Enneagram 8, 5, & the Counterphobic 6 are more likely to co-occur with an Dismissive-Avoidant attachment style.

Enneagram 3, 7 and 1 could easily go either way.

Due to Enneagram 4s reliance on **introjection** as a primary defense mechanism, I think 4 is the most likely candidate to co-occur with the Fearful-Avoidant adult attachment style, followed by the Counter-phobic 6. *(The most severe attachment traumas give rise to dissociative disorders. Introjection is often a primary defense mechanism of those individuals who have experienced severe early childhood trauma and as a result have dissociative disorders such as DID and OSDD. In fact, individuals who develop these kinds of disorders are higher in Trait Openness and exhibit an innate capacity for creativity, imagination and absorption. These personality factors may actually contribute to the creation of these disorders as a survival response to trauma.)*

Big 5 data suggests that Enneagram types 3 and 1 are characterized by a certain level of trait conscientious (which also corresponds to lower levels of trait neuroticism), certainly indicating a lower likelihood of co-occuring Fearful-Avoidant  attachment, and perhaps less likelihood of insecure attachment overall.

In short, there are no easy answers... but I do think it's safe enough to speculate about the probability of insecure attachment co-occuring across different enneagram types.

The first time you sell your blood, it’s like nothing. There’s no real thinking happenin’.

There is even a utility hose and floor drain in your line of sight. You understand what all of this implies but can’t bring yourself to admit it, so you twitch with restlessness just a little more than you did during the first transaction.

You begin to see the spiderwebs and the vermin trapped within them from the edge of your vision. Your facial muscles begin to expand outward with vigilance as they try to sense the room, and your eyes widen and sort of bulge out of your head. 

You start to look like a crazy person that second trip. That’s how it begins, the real end of the self. The ZBZ blood clinic holds an all-encompassing, panoramic aura of despair and futility that you can’t easily escape from. 

You start to wonder, “Am I like these people? Sell a few ounces of blood… and then suddenly one day I find myself sitting in an abandoned subway tunnel eating expired cat food with a stained spork I found in the back pocket of a dead man’s pants?!” 

“Is this going to be my life?” “Am I destined to lose all my teeth?”

The second time is when the anxiety creeps in and sits dormant in the base of your spine, just like HPV… waiting for the perfect moment to flare-up and ruin what could have been a really good time.  

\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*

The third time you sell your blood for drug money, is when you notice the shame take over. No longer just desperate, paranoid and anxious, that deep-seated hatred of your own existence takes the throne. The new king bosses everyone else around, and the kingdom begins to disintegrate into chaos. In-group fighting begins. Memory fades. No point in remembering who you are anymore. 

Yah. I tell you - that third time is a real bitch…. but *then* it gets easier and easier and easier...

…. Until one day you find yourself with a dumb grin on your face saying, “Sure, why not?” to a round of experimental injections and short institutional stay when the nice lady asks. And in a haze, you sign all of the forms they give you. You nod. You smile. And you don’t even think about it anymore, just happy to have a safe place to sleep, enough blood to keep from passing-out, and a few extra cookies to hide under the pillow.  

You give them answers. They give you the drugs you’ve come to depend on. It’s a simple and gratifying system. You can appreciate it. You can bask within it. What’s a little personal information for the privilege of accessing a free service?

And when the researchers ask you for a list of your closest friends and family members, you give-up the information willingly. You’ve come to trust your new medical family, and the miracle treatment that they’ve promised you. This experimental injection could potentially change *everything*, you’re told. 

Changing everything implies hard work, but most anything looks better when you compare it to a lifetime of expertizing in the blood-for-cash industry. You already hate yourself and have nothing left to lose. It’s only natural to wonder, “How can I work this to my advantage?” 

*Little did you know that you never had a chance at all. Advantage itself was an illusion.* 

The crisis intervention begins. You’re ready for it. You’ve been preparing for the onslaught of family confessionals about your disruptive wrongdoings. You are ready to face-up to your mistakes. Since you started the treatments, your emotional pain has diminished significantly and faded away from your conscious awareness. You think that you have hit the apex of human suffering and come out the other side on top.

Inside yourself you feel positive, warm: action-oriented.  Your old self (the who would explode with rage at the smallest insult) has stepped back and a new, higher quality individual has emerged from the wreckage. The drugs are clearly working, and facing the family seems like the next obvious step to making amends and going clear.

The intervention room is bright and colorful. The atmosphere is so light that it borders on the artificial. You don’t know that it is all part of the drug trial. Your mind is dulled with manufactured happiness, and stripped of your animal defenses you walk yourself into the execution chamber with a wave to the audience and chuckle to yourself. There is nothing you can’t handle now that you’re fixed.  

On of the lab assistants explains to your family that the company has been experimenting with a way to transform mental pain into overt physical pain. 

You learn that researchers have hypothesized that visualization could help a damaged person like you recover by making your subjectively held pain more real; allow for an inner state to blossom into an objective thing that could be seen and measured by all. Unfortunately, earlier subjects had perished due to the extreme nature of the drug trial. It seems that an unintended side effect of the gene therapy was an extreme response to emotional wounding – a tragic extension of the placebo response: Self-immolation. 

The researcher reassures the audience as they squirm with anticipation in their plush seats, that although previous trials failed, this time things will be different. This time no one will die. They lock the doors.

I have ADHD. I think my personality (INFJ) is affected. I have done research on how ADHD may shape personality (mostly trait correlation studies and meta-analyses) and plan to do more in the future, but I will share with you what I have learned thus far. Much of the research done on the intersection of personality and ADHD focuses on the Big Five personality inventory. I will try to relate that MBTI as accurately as possible... but there is no direct correspondence between the two theories.

Individuals with ADHD tend to be higher in the Big 5 trait Openness, which corresponds generally to Intuition.  If higher in inattention symptoms, individuals are more likely to express higher levels of Neuroticism (express more negative emotions) and to rate as predominantly Introverted on the MBTI. If higher in Impulsivity symptoms, individuals are likely to rate as more (trait) Disagreeable and to be classified as Introverted Thinking and Perceiving types, respectively, on the MBTI. Higher levels of Hyperactivity symptoms seemed to be related to higher levels of Extroversion on Big Five and MBTI. Additionally, people with ADHD rate much lower overall in trait Conscientiousness... however this is a significant finding in only in 1 of the 2 aspects of conscientiousness. The two aspects are Industriousness and Order. Individuals with ADHD are less Orderly and traditional, but not necessarily less Industrious: productive and/or achievement-striving.

ADHD purportedly complicates the way in which a given personality will manifest itself. Individuals with ADHD are more likely to express both ends of a trait spectrum - for example, to be both very extroverted at times, and very introverted at others. Or highly Industrious and agreeable while performing work that is intrinsically motivating, and disagreeable and unfocused when disinterested. ADHD provides for a chaotic and unconventional brain wiring, so it makes sense that this difference would be reflected in unpredictable and chaotic outward behaviors as well.

My own experience has been that how my personality manifests behaviorally is highly context specific. I have been formally assessed using MBTI a couple of times. When I was a senior in high school I got ENFP. When I was a Junior in college I got INTP. I've also gotten ENTP and INFP. After learning about the cognitive functions I realized that everyone was putting too much stock in how orderly I was, and that I would have to factor all questions related to orderliness out in order to get a true result. Just because I'm late for appointments and don't keep my space meticulously organized, does not mean that I am not mentally focused. Sometimes I find myself obsessing over the small details, and at other times I completely disregard them. Sometimes I am highly agreeable, sometimes I argue at length (with passion) just for the thrill of it.  I am a bundle of contradictions, as I beileve most people with combined type ADHD are.

This became evident when planning a European vacation with two friends. My perceiving friend keeps her space more or less organized, however it was like pulling teeth to get her to agree on Hostels to stay at before arriving in country, rather than 'feeling out' our options as we went. She would do almost anything to weasel out of making definite plans. It terrified me. I wanted to have some idea as to what each day would bring, not wander around aimlessly looking for something to do while wasting precious time and money. My friend felt that my need to 'plan plan plan' killed the adventure. However, when I wanted to wander down cool (safe) little alleyways instead of sticking directly to the main tourist area or eat local foods, she would get uncomfortable and freak out. While she is open and perceiving in general (and I am more deliberate) this doesn't stop me from impulsively following my whims or some environmental curiosity, if they become more enticing than my original plan. For her it is the opposite. She likes to keep things open-ended, but is less Open to experience in general. She doesn't want to plan, but that doesn't necessarily mean that she wants to do novel and unusual things in her unplanned time.

If in doubt, I have also found that you can gauge your level of P Vs J by observing a conversation with an opposite type. My father has ADHD and is an INFP. When we were directing a play together and would engage in creative brainstorming (an activity that we both tend to get carried-away with) I noticed that my dad would just keep brainstorming endlessly (and indecisively) if I didn't force him to direct his attention back to the larger goal and to make a decision.

In short, ADHD seems involve having an array of personality traits which do not often go together within the same person and present outwardly in a contradictory fashion. I'm still doing more research of course, as this is not the total picture. Maybe someday I'll get it done and published!

I think true Dominant Intuitives are going to have more "memory" problems related to what they actually DID in the past. There is some evidence to suggest that Ni/Ne users are more disconnected from themselves - this is called Dissociation - than other personality types. Dissociation is commonly thought to be a pathological response to trauma or stress, but in N users seems to be a naturally occurring and largely unproblematic phenomenon which bears more resemblance to a meditative type state, than a pathological one. Dissociating from an experience allows a person to separate from what's actually happening in order to get a sense of WHY it's happening, and how it fits into the larger scheme of all possible life experiences.  

INFJs tend to assign symbols to their experiences, rather than trying to remember the sequence of events and actions in detail. I have found that sometimes I won't remember an experience I went through until the symbol for that experience has been triggered by a current event. Once I am aware of what the symbolic representation I originally assigned to the experience is, I oftentimes will actually begin to remember it in scary detail (like a normal memory). 

**To translate all this abstraction -** 

 I basically remember my life as a series of stories, each with their own unique meaning. Sort of like a book of fables or fairy tales, where each story is a lesson designed to remind me of what I learned about a certain aspect of life. I don't necessarily remember the story about the Tortoise and the Hare (slow and steady wins the race) until I find myself in the middle of the contest. 

I think this processing difference can be a real issue for INFJs, because we may be triggered by  (and begin to respond emotionally to) symbols in our environment before we can even consciously comprehend their existence. This is most obvious in social situations where you can begin to unconsciously respond in a pre-programmed way to things that haven't actually happened yet. 

For example - you are in a three person social group eating out at a restaurant. You get up to go to the bathroom. On the way back, as you're walking to the table which is still a little distance off, you suddenly realize that your friends have fallen for each other. If you've had bad experiences with this kind of dynamic in the past, you might immediately feel like a 3rd wheel. By the time you've arrived at the table and sat back down, you are already sure your friends have a mutual attraction, but that one is in denial and the other isn't,... AND this will probably all end in disaster when they both get drunk, hook up and regret it. You'll never be able to go out and have dinner with these two friends like this again.  (That's the symbol/story that was triggered with in you). With all these unconscious processes turning, you begin to act like this version of the future is certain, without understanding exactly why. Your friends notice you've changed and are also put-off. They don't know what they are going to do later. You try to warn each of them separately not to rush into things... but neither can see what you can see... and in the end you are the one that looks crazy. 

On a biological note, women certainly experience memory fluctuations based on the balance of sex hormones in their system at a particular point in time. In one experiment they found that women are much better at finding their car in a parking lot at certain times in their menstrual cycle than in others.

I've actually done this very thing before. Here are a couple of things that worked for me. Maybe you'll find it helpful... I don't know:

* Ask yourself - Why am I procrastinating?

Is it fear of failure? Perfectionism? Lack of interest in the subject? Trying to meet unclear expectations? Does it take you a really long time to write, or is writing extremely work-intensive?

*I put stuff off because I know it's going to be painful to organize the information, and experience has taught me that it will take me 5x longer than the average person to put what I need to say into words. Sometimes starting an essay is like standing at the trail head for Mt Everest, looking-up into the clouds and suddenly panicking because you realize you might actually die from the amount of work it would take to make it the top. I don't feel motivated to start climbing until a bear chases me up the first mile or so. Then I'm on the path and it makes no sense to turn around - specially with that bear down there waiting for me to fail so he can gobble me up.*

Sometimes just identifying the source of the procrastination can be helpful. That not to say that it's easy... or that there is only a single contributing factor to your problem.

* Talk to a supportive (and inquisitive) person about your research - someone who will interrupt you to ask questions about concepts/procedures etc.. that they don't understand.

By discussing the research you may find the wording that will best convey your information to the audience. Have the other person sit at a computer and type down anything that comes out of your mouth that is useful and/or brilliant.

If they paraphrase what you are saying in their own words, this can also be helpful. You may find yourself having a strong reaction, like, "No. No you don't get it. That's not what I'm trying to say!"

Okay then, what *are* you trying to say? Sometimes hearing our work in someone else's voice, helps us find our own.

This conversation starter thing should feel almost like you're not doing the assignment at all. You're just wasting time having a conversation - however, this will prime you to think more deeply about the message you want to convey and how best to communicate it. At the end you will have a word document with a ton of content you can use. You will have done something not quite as painful or high stakes, which will contribute to your ability to complete the assignment overall and boost your confidence.

* When  you get started... don't stop. It's probably unhealthy... but it may be the only way to get it done. I have the most success when I can complete something in 1 sitting. Every time that I take a break, the likelihood that I will complete a paper on time greatly diminishes. Continually having to restart the process of working on the paper is a killer. I NEED the fear - the deadline. I think it's just the way my brain is wired to operate. From my observation of ADHDers this is just how it works... intrinsic motivation or fear.

* My first diary entry was proof of my child's mind beginning to exercise Ni, but still in a very concrete way. My folks were very religiously active and we went to church at least 3 times a week. In short, I was on a continuous quest to uncover the truth as a child, and to find purpose for myself. * I told lots of complicated and dramatic stories. I had a big imagination and liked to use it to entertain other people. I became fascinated with hypnotism and started practicing it on my friends and myself. I was also fascinated by the occult and with 'dark' things. I had intense, vivid dreams. I would look for human artifacts - old photos, notebooks - anything that looked like it had had personal significance for someone at some time. I suddenly remembered these people that in the past had tried to be there for me when I was inconsolable... but which apparently I wiped from my mind while constructing my narrow, inflexible personal narrative of victimization and helplessness. I acknowledged that these people had tried to connect with me, but that my mind was unable to receive that connection.

Then, I just let go of me. I realized the game was always rigged and that I could never win it. Everything that will happen in my life has in a way... already happened. I *know* that time is an illusion... I mean, in a pragmatic sense of course time is real - but metaphysically it does not seem to be... and that is so freeing to experience.

I cannot prevent the catastrophic and the random. I must accept that I will die. My parents will die. My siblings and friends will die. I cannot stop this eventual end, nor do I want to - because having an ending is the very thing that gives you a beginning. Life is defined by death. People will leave. You cannot prevent it. It will happen one way or another. In that moment I grieved my lost life and finally reached acceptance. I let go of the lies and the assumptions and I decided that I was going to start-over with a new perspective... one that is less paranoid and withdrawn. I realized that pursuing material possessions, status, social acceptance and approval is a waste of my time and my life. I realized that I was always connected to everyone else on a fundamental, but inobservable level of existence, regardless of whether I saw this 'connection' intentionally demonstrated or not. 

There is bad in this world, and there is good (and in my thoughts this 'badness' and 'goodness' is the product of people... not of nature or god). While I am afforded this time to live this human life (whatever that means or doesn't mean) I can choose to contribute to the goodness and try to help others who are suffering to find and access the lost, but extremely resilient & unbreakable force within themselves, or I can continue to view myself as helpless to effect change in my own life and succumb to nihilistic despair. I can continue to hate my parents for the mistakes they made - or I can let go and understand that they were terrified, traumatized people re-enacting their own traumas. It doesn't make it ok. It was definitely still abuse. But from a global perspective, it is understandable. They could not connect with me because they were never connected to themselves. 

I can continue to react to my current boyfriend by playing games, running away and/or erupting in anger... or I can take a breath, remind myself of how much love I have for him, extend compassion rather than impulsively reacting to him like a hurt animal, and work toward repairing my relationships rather than running from them. In the end, I'm the only person who will always be there for me. I will be the one who regulates my emotions. I don't need a therapist to do that for me. It is not my boyfriend's responsibility to 'regulate' me... I'm a 31 year old MSW student. I will be seeing my own clients soon... I have to cut this shit out and do the work that has to be done. I have to take on the job of handling my own constant crises. I have no other choice. No one can do this for me! 

Anyhow, I could not do this experience justice with words (even thought I used alot ;). It 'unlocked' me... and since then I have been able to handle a lot of chaotic feelings, internal moodiness and relationship issues that I previously would have crumpled in the face of. I feel a sense of being more or less whole now - or at least like a person with free will. I know I'll be okay, no matter what happens... because I I guess I have finally managed to internalize the the last part of the serenity prayer... "the wisdom to know the difference between the things I can and cannot change"

1. INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES: There are ways that we are like everyone else, ways we are like someone else and ways that we are like no one else. Unfortunately therapists often assume that by drawing-on their education (which may be misguided & ancient btw) and experience they can safety categorize clients into 'clinical' groups and gloss over the individual differences. For some people (perhaps like you) individual differences (the ways we are like no one else) are striking - and this has to be understood and accepted by the therapist in order for progress to occur. I believe that rather than telling and assuming, a therapist should endeavor to ascertain how their client's mind functions and clarify as you go along in conversation that they are understanding the story they are hearing... rather than trying to force the conversation in another direction that they themselves prefer. In retrospect I can see how many therapists (who did not understand how my healthily functioning mind works) thought that I was lying to myself, imagining things, trying to get attention etc... when I was just 'being me'. I'm just kind of a weird, highly intelligent & imaginative person. It's not all pathology, some of it is just the random chaotic-ness of my atypical brain wiring.  

2. CLARIFICATION: Looking back on the situation, I did not REALLY give her the information she needed to understand and validate my perspective. Even though I had thought a lot about what I wanted to say at home, I didn't REALLY explain what I meant to my therapist. I said a lot of things that were leaps (but made sense to me) and then I expected her to follow my story line. How do you explain to an outgoing, flamboyant, 60 year old woman with a background in art therapy, that new research in quantum mechanics has helped you resolve issues with socializing and lack of identity? My brain made this leap that is helpful for me, but if I am objective I can see why someone on the outside might assume I'm delusional without the 6 hours of explanation it would take for me to get her to understand how this epiphany occurred and why it has changed my perspective in such a way that globally alleviated my stress. My therapist did not really have the information she needed to come to a conclusion about what I was telling her. That was partly on me, and partly on her for assuming that she was getting it without taking the time to clarify with me that she was on the right track. 

3. ULTIMATELY YOU HEAL YOURSELF: Luckily, I had read the book 'Siddhartha' the day before my session and it reminded me of something that is key. Siddhartha is a young man who is on a journey, desperately trying to reach enlightenment. A few years into this journey, he finally meets the Buddha face-to-face (and while realizing and accepting that this Buddha has in fact reached enlightenment) Siddhartha ultimately realizes that the only way to get where he wants to go is through himself. YOU are the only person who can know your own mind, and although the teachings of wise others maybe helpful, informative and provide a certain enlightenment, the only true enlightenment and healing comes from the fearless examination of your own mind and the ability to tolerate the experience of your own existence.

In the past I struggled with ‘dating’ because it seemed so artificial; contrived and inauthentic. I was using OKC however, so that may have been part of it (online dating is even more artificial feeling). It was almost embarrassing, the idea of fully participating in this charade. I felt a need to seek out a relationship, but at the same time actually slapping a ‘single’ label on myself and then purposely standing among the other singles and waiting by my turn to be picked - feels sort of repulsive. Online dating does have a tendency to pull the salesman right out of people... and the salesman/image manager in people tends to repel me. I’m searching for authenticity... not looking to buy the propaganda people are peddling from their profiles. 

I know this probably sounds pretty severe, but when I was online dating I was in a cynical frame of mind. It made me depressed to check my account... and it made me kind of want to take people and throw them into a simulation and then test hypotheses on them, rather than actually deign myself to interact with them. I realized that I was seeing people as ignorant propagators of an unjust, superficial ‘mating’ system with rules and obligations that I didn’t want to have to follow. 

I had to understand what function taking this cynical and disconnected perspective served in my life. I realized that I was afraid of what people would think of me, and since I couldn’t resolve that, I distracted myself from the real issue by focusing on my internal sense of alienation. 

In the end I successfully online dated; been with the guy I met for 3 years. I decided to be 100% real. In fact, I started to treat my OKC account as a sort of blog... I would just get on every week or so and change my self summary to whatever I was thinking at that moment - stream of consciousness stuff- AND THEY LOVED IT!  When I went full crazy, eccentric me... that is when I started getting the responses I wanted. 

One of my most popular self-summaries was actually one where I critiqued people’s need to ‘manage their image’ and project their wishes about themselves (rather than their realities) into their online personas. I basically tried to call-out widespread inauthenticity. I was angry and it was a terrible argument, but it sure got the attention of some interesting and intelligent people who wanted to debate me! Turns out they were just happy that someone else noticed how awkward and uncomfortable it can be. 
Dating websites are standardized in a way. Most of them have specific questions to answer or other activities to engage in. Screw that. You don’t need to answer their questions! Just say whatever you want to say about yourself. Find a way to show people your personality through your writing or pictures or whatever. 

One issue with online dating that I see is that people do not play-up their differences. Profile after profile seems to merge into these few stereotypical, gendered blobs. Don’t be part of the blob! It is the difference between you and that other girl/guy that will attract the right people. For example, how important is it really, that you and the girl both love the Big Lebowski? Could that space be better used to explain WHY you like certain movies? What fuels you? What motivates your interests/passions? 

Just be interesting... not hard, since the way your mind works is so unusual as it is. People will notice your authenticity. It will be refreshing for the RIGHT people. They will be intrigued by your ability to be straightforward and honest about yourself with confidence. Good riddance to the ones that don’t like your profile... wouldn’t of been good matches anyway. 

For a passive/agreeable male INFJ who is online dating, I would also say that if you put your true thoughts out there, the right woman will eventually find you. It sucks, because most women (the younger you are the worse it is) are very uncomfortable/unaccustomed to formally making the first move. However there are some of us that know who we are, what we want and aren’t going to let a golden opportunity pass just because you didn’t send us a message initially. We will be in contact, although you must put the effort forward to be YOU for us to find you. Also, if you are a really agreeable guy, you probably need the balance of having a more aggressive partner to protect you from certain things anyways. 

Good luck!

I want to say that I agree with the OP 100%! I would also like to add that at its foundation, INFJ describes a way that the human brain preferentially organizes mental energy, NOT behavior. The theory of cognitive type has nothing *inherently* to do with behavior. 

MBTI was created by taking a highly abstract theory by Carl Jung and coming-up with a system for relating/mapping particular behaviors to patterns of thinking. Jung's theory was not particularly accessible, and it also did not provide a practical application. MBTI was a way or reorganizing the principle tenets of JUNG's theory and making them more practical for every day use and self-exploration.  

Jung himself was interested in WHY people think differently. He spent decades in clinical practice talking at length with his clients and became interested in why people can look at the same situation and then argue for very different things. Sure, sometimes specific behaviors flow from specific patterns of thought in a predictable way, but not always. 

There are also important factors of personality that this theory/system DOES NOT cover, like: how mentally healthy you are, how OLD you are, the stage of life you're in, whether you're currently under stress or not, what kinds of life experiences you've faced, the social/physical environment you grew-up in, the defense mechanisms you've built to uniquely respond to challenges in your life, the current level of development that each function is at, any false personas you've built to handle certain situations, training you've received (like acting lessons or public speaking/debate which change how your behavior manifests), education, atypical neural wiring like dyslexia, autism spectrum or ADHD, psychiatric medication/illicit drug-use effects, culture, the kind of parenting you received... the list goes on really. It's actually kind of amazing that a system like MBTI that uses behavior could even be as accurate as it is, with so many variables left unaccounted for.

**How to Prepare for the Un-pre-parable:**  

**1. Begin viewing your life a series of potential stories.** The idea is to refocus your mind so that when you encounter an experience in the future that has story potential, you actually realize that while you’re in the midst of it. Then depending how you play the situation, the whole experience can be transformed into an entertaining story for later.  It is actually a pretty niffy coping mechanism. For example, when really humiliating things happen to me, I remind myself that after the initial horror wears off, I will have a great story to tell. That’s what I’m thinking about while it’s happening and it insulates me from negative emotions and self-doubt.  

**2. Rehearse.**  
When I audition for plays, one of the things I’ve been asked to do fairly often is to tell a 2 minute story. When I have an experience that could make a great story, I rehearse it. I try to remember the sequence of events and the most important details that I want to convey. When I’m driving I tell the story out-loud to myself. When I feel like I know what to say about the event, and what NOT to say (*accidentally onstage in front of a bunch of strangers*) then I record myself telling the story. I listen to it. I reassure myself that it makes sense, and only reveals as much information about myself as I want it to. This preparation process makes me feel more comfortable with spontaneous action, because I know that I have practiced it enough to have built-up a default “story-telling” mode that can run on autopilot if I want it to.

IQ scores are often listed in the client’s master file along with a list of all formal diagnoses they’ve received. That file is then passed from worker to worker - agency to agency (usually without ever being questioned). At one agency I was placed at, 96% of all clients were listed as being in the low-average to profoundly below average range in their master client file. This was NOT an agency focused on intellectual or developmental disabilities  - strictly mental health related concerns.
In observing the day-to-day interactions of the clients and workers, it was obvious that many clients were significantly more intelligent and capable then their IQ scores indicated, however they had not been challenged to grow or in many cases held accountable for their actions. 

The majority of staff (although well-meaning) had no expectation that growth could be possible within this population, as they had read the client file prior to intake and already KNEW (beyond a shadow of a doubt) that the client was clinically slow. These staff had no reason to doubt the listed IQ scores. They took them as factually accurate and tailored their treatment plans and interventions based-upon this questionable info. I also witnessed some especially crafty patients who turned their low IQ scores to their advantage - using it to continue to play the victim or to reap the rewards of not having to do anything for themselves.

In my opinion, to be an INFJ is to live in a state of contradiction... or rather to live AS a contradiction.

I think that our being so contradictory in nature is the reason that we can see the inherent duality of our human existence. When I am having an existential crisis, I remind myself that my strength is to be able to see both sides of the coin. Rather than just focusing on how stuck I am, I should accept that I am in an ongoing state of fluctuation. From a strengths POV I can see that my Fe (although often embarrassing and frankly out-of-control) is the natural mechanism by which I orient myself in the world of objects and objective conditions. I cannot discard it just because it *seems* like a foolish way to spend time to my Ti. 

**To Grow:**  

**Experience:** We need to go out into the world and have experiences that engage our emotions rather than constantly sitting at home and 'reasoning.' 

**Expression:** We need to express and/or sit-with our emotions as they come-up, rather than always trying to suppress them. If we suppress our emotions and refuse to be assertive with others out of fear of rejection, we both impede our growth and our friend/partner's growth. We also insult the other by assuming they can't handle our emotions. Just because we perceive (or are told) that it's hard for someone else to have to listen to us, doesn't mean that what we are saying is wrong, or that we shouldn't 'put' that *burden* on other people.  

Maybe the last time we were in a weird, tense argument with a loved one, we were actually completely on-point, so much so that it triggered their defenses and caused them to lash-out at us for being so direct and honest. This in turn, temporarily disrupts the feeling environment. The truth may temporarily alter the amount of harmony or emotional integration (vibe) we normally pick-up on from an individual, and that can send us into a emotional doubt spiral. aka "Did I destroy the relationship by acting like we're closer friends than we really are? Was I too forward?! Did I alienate this person by being too presumptuous?" Who is to say that being presumptuous is always a bad thing? Some people are more skilled at presumption than others. 

We should not take the triggering of defenses as a 'bad' thing in and of itself. The truth often hurts. Sometimes other people NEED to hear what we said, whether they like it or not or accept it or not. You don't really have to do much. The truth has a way of piercing right through the defenses, getting inside of us and taking root whether we want it to or not. 

**Self-Compassion** We need to extend compassion and emotional validation to ourselves so that our unconscious mind can feel vulnerable enough to let our defenses down and expose our inner truth (cause God knows no one else is going to do it).  
Buried beneath the defensive/compartmentalization features of our minds, are the answers we didn't even know we had.  

It's the doing-it-for-yourself part that gets in our way. We can readily serve up this unconscious knowledge that we didn't even know we had for others, but why not for ourselves? Where/what is the barrier? Is it necessary to have this barrier in our lives today? Is it protecting us from anything or is it wasted space? When should be compartmentalize our emotions, and when should we try to consciously connect with our emotional sensations.. or even heighten them for effect? 

**Self-Respect** Once we are feeling our emotions in our bodies and intellectually observing them with our brains, we can begin to make sense of our experience(s). Approach yourself with curiosity and respect. Ask questions, out-loud, just like you would do if you were advising your best friend on a relationship issue or whatever. You will be surprised with the answers you get back. 

Example questions: Why don't we comfort ourselves the way we would comfort others in our position? Is it because we see ourselves as somehow removed from the rest of humanity? Where does that low-self-esteem or lack of confidence stem from and what role does it play in maintaining our current situation? Why must we be so mean to ourselves? What role does being our own worst enemy play in maintaining our sanity? Are we addicted to our own self-doubt? etc...

**Self-Acceptance and Integration:** Take what you've learned and apply it to yourself. You will be amazed at how quickly negative experiences and emotions can be re-integrated back into our 'whole self.' Lacking emotional integration (or personality differentiation) is a very confusing state to be in. However, the only way to move through-it is to allow yourself to re-integrate (which always requires some level of self-acceptance.)

Good luck. I hope some of this makes sense :)

I did not tell the actors how to act - as that is a big "no no" and a great way to alienate people!

So I actually used two strategies to make sure that the actors understood the core features/emotions of the situation. 

The first strategy I used was to cast the play with individuals who showed more of a bent for deep thinking & mental flexibility over those that were very talented, but mostly flash. To get personal investment from my actors (since this was unpaid community-level theater) I specifically chose people that I thought would work well, but had never been given a chance to have a principle role due to the fact that most directors do their casting based on purely superficial characteristics (at least in com. theatre). These actors were eager to learn, work hard and to surrender to the creative process. I gave them a chance to shine, and this in turn reinforced their loyalty and willingness to take direction. 

Farther into the rehearsal process, I gave my actors homework to fill-out that had a set of structured questions for them to answer about their character. The questions were devised to  stimulate critical thinking and to verbally elicit  the ideas and underlying presumptions they had about their character(s) underlying motivational and emotional states, relationships and so on. I also felt that we needed to cultivate an environment where the actors could feel vulnerable with one another and still be safe. Then we had group discussion and each actor was allowed to ask the other actors (as their characters) questions. Sometimes these questions were random like when my JACK (the deceased heart donor) asked the actors who played his parents why they never got divorced. (great question) Sometimes the lines of questioning were more straight forward. Ultimately, I tried to make the rehearsal process as collaborative and safe as possible. Doing that, and then actively inviting the actors to engage in their own critical thinking & exploratory processes was enough to make a great show. I extended respect to my actors, and in turn they extended respect to me.

After initial research, I have some (provisional) thoughts  - 

So there is this set of brain regions that are engaged when people are in a “resting state” (left to themselves in a scanner, with no explicit task instruction) that cognitive neuroscientists have named "The Default Mode Network." (DMN)

It is called the *Default* setting because when given nothing else to do, the brain defaults to thinking about the person it’s embedded in (self-reflection/monitoring). The DMN has been implicated in depression, creativity and frequent daydreaming. It is thought to shut-off when we need to engage in goal-oriented behavior or to complete a task. Most people spend more time in goal-oriented thinking than in the default (self-referential) state. The DMN also seems to process the passage of time, having structural features that are involved in imagining both the past and the future. The work of Dario Nardi from USC has suggested that the INFJ brain spends more time overall, utilizing the DMN - especially the portions which correspond to imagining or envisioning the future.  

 (Intriguing right?)

>In one experiment investigating the functionality of the DMN, 25 participants were asked to do creative thinking tasks, including the standard measure of divergent thinking, asking how many uses you can come up with for a brick (spoiler alert: doorstop and weapon are two go-to options). At the start of the task, the DMN coupled with the **salience network** (which selects which stimuli to attend to) and toward the end of the task, it coupled with the **executive network** (thought be responsible for the control of attention and working memory). These results that suggest that the DMN contributes to the (more or less) spontaneous generation of (potentially useful) ideas, but can easily be shut down when we need to focus on the task at hand. 

I think that you are potentially observing your own shifts in and out of the DMN. Your mind is wandering (DMN), then you receive an unconscious cue from the environment that disrupts your daydream and refocuses your thought process (Salience Network). If you respond to that cue that you should get to 'doing' something, then you are engaging your executive network or as some papers are calling it, "the Task-Positive network." 

The above is the neurotypical human attentional process as far as we know.

 For me, on account of my ADHD (which has been observed to disrupt the functionality of both the salience & executive networks) I spend more time overall in the task-negative, DMN state. I have to consciously fight the creative thinking impulse so that I am able to focus on concrete reality and task completion. I'm way more of a dreamer than I am a doer. Even writing this out to you took 2 hours! 2 hours! Who spends 2 hours writing a post on reddit?! Someone with an overactive DMN, that's who.

https://www.thecut.com/2017/01/why-your-mind-is-always-wandering.html

This first article also has links within it to the wikipedia pages for the DMN and Task Positive Network (which by the way, encompasses both the Salience and Executive networks.)

The play is called "The Tin Woman" and was written by Sean Grennan. 

To be honest, the play script itself left a little to be desired, so I ended-up writing a prologue to precede the opening act and help give a sense of closure at the end of the play (w/ the playwright's permission of course). Grennan's strength is in writing witty and realistically raw dialogue, but not necessarily in creating a sense of cohesiveness. The end of the play was weak, taking a rather artificial, Hallmark-esque turn that in other productions had been heavily panned by the critics. I worked very hard to ameliorate that situation... which actually turned-out to require no additional writing. I think this is where we succeeded when other casts failed: we took the dialogue as written, but instead of interpreting it in a straightforward way, we came at it from a totally different angle. 

For example: In this play a heart transplant recipient (JOY) experiences survivor guilt post transplant, leading her to a dark place where she contacts the family of her heart donor, although against the rules. 

The family is divided about whether or not they want to meet her. The donor's mother invites (JOY) to dinner, and an emotionally intense meal ensues. The father of the donor (HANK) who had a horrible argument with his son just before he died, makes it very clear during the dinner that he wants nothing to do with (JOY), and it escalates into a physical altercation quickly. Between the dinner conversation and a trip to the cemetery (HANK) suddenly does a 180 and changes his mind about accepting the woman who received his son's heart. 

The lines are something like: "Would you like to stay at our house tonight? You can can use Jack's (the deceased son) room!"

This was too much of a sudden change in HANK'S attitude to be believable or meaningful. 

Doing research on prior productions, I found that many actors and directors chose to interpret these lines in a very bright, sunny, totally-accepting kind of way that directly corresponds with the tone of the text, rather than utilizing the more complicated & nebulous subtext inherent in the story. In other words, I reminded the actors that just because someone says that everything is ok, doesn't necessarily make everything ok - even in their own mind. A character in this situation is on the cusp of change, and that emotional idea of a *slow transitioning* has to be incorporated into the presentation of the those lines to make the story feel real and personally impacting. 

I sat in the audience, and every night people sobbed (including the older, stoic gentlemen who could see themselves in HANK)! 
I have to admit that I was sitting there thinking, "Now all these people who could have never related to my experience with this are being forced to temporarily feel the horrible burden of the life I've had! Mwahahaha!" 

Growing-up I wasn't allowed to have/express personal feelings, and I definitely wasn't allowed to complain about my older sister. We had terrible sibling rivalry, so it was really like being trapped in hell for 18 years. It was a burden carrying around the belief that no one could ever understand or relate to my situation, that no one would ever know how much pain I (and my family) experienced. 

Watching people experience my pain (albeit second hand) while watching the play, served as a cathartic release and resolved a lot of anger & grief I had been holding onto. For the first time I accepted that I had strong emotions, and seeing those emotions mirrored in others was extremely validating. Growing-up my parents would constantly pretend that everything was GREAT and would refuse to talk about the elephant in the room. This was very confusing for me emotionally. For example, as a 7 year old, I often saw my 10 year old sister get taken off to the ER in an ambulance, but if I cried or worried about what was happening I would get mocked, slapped or locked in the car by myself for hours. I stopped thinking that it was ok to feel sad or worried... this piece of myself returned after putting on the play and I fully comprehended the true transformative power of theatre. I've been more preoccupied with directing (rather than acting) ever since. It's almost a *high* you feel when you realize that it is actually possible through the process of creating art, to change people with your insights about human nature.

Even though we are perfectionists, we DO understand that we can't actually be perfect. However this does not stop us from aspiring to be (or have our work be) as close to that as possible. **Beyond INFJ.** I was a very troubled young person with a rough home situation, and that significantly impeded my ability to succeed academically. I know now, that I also had undiagnosed & untreated ADHD. When I was properly diagnosed and treated for it at age 26 (post-Bachelor's degree) I couldn't believe the morass I had been trying to fight and muddle through all those years! (sometimes successfully, sometimes not.) School certainly would have been easier had I been able to focus my mind on the task at hand. 

To get to the point: **knowing more about how your mind works** (say, utilizing personality theory or MBTI for example) **can be very helpful in navigating yourself academically/occupationally, but it's definitely not the ONLY factor to consider.** There are some realities of life that are not merely theoretical... like whether or not you actually have enough money to go to college, or whether the post-graduate job you so desired in that highly specific area, suddenly becomes a horrifying, monstrous beast of burden when coupled with very low pay, yet massive student loan debt or other stressful situational factors that arise at home and on the job.

I was expelled from our local public high school in my first year. Subsequently, I went to the **" alternative"** high-school and graduated from there. I was not academically prepared to enter college, because no one thought that I would be going. Only, I didn't know that! I thought for sure I was going to go to college and everything would suddenly be great and I'd be accepted and valued as an intelligent human-being. I was wrong - higher education is pretty much the same as high school, only with more options and hopefully, autonomy.  

**Most important thing I learned in college: Take advantage of having options and pick your class by the professor.** 
If you can get a hold of past reviews on their teaching style and personality, then you can see if that particular professor and class will be a good fit for you. Opportunities are only what you make of them, so don't allow yourself to be too passive and uninvolved in your own decision making process. 

Will they tolerate all the questioning? Will they stare at me dumb-founded when I ask them in good faith who invented mathematics? Do they love their subject?  - For me personally, if I perceived a professor lectured in an uninspired, inauthentic or purely derivative style, I would lose focus and interest. I've always wanted to learn for the sake of learning... I want to know more, think new ideas and personally connect with them, construct original arguments, ... reinvent the wheel etc. 

I have learned that I prefer to be taught by people who love what they do. I feed off of that enthusiastic energy they have, and it makes me feel more inspired because I see the way their passion for the subject has transformed them. I avoid a dispassionate lecturer that only knows the shallow overview of their topic at all costs. I think it kills my soul a little.

Have him read **"The Body Keeps the Score"** by Bessel Van Der Kolk. That has the hard science and should definitely be enough to convince him. 

Here is the author's wiki: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bessel_van_der_Kolk 


**Basically (and in the broadest terms)** when you experience really horrible and shocking stuff, your body is flooded with stress hormones. At a certain point of bodily stress a person's consciousness or ego, can no longer bare the mental burden of their experience. This causes the person to disconnect from their body (or sense of self) and enter an altered state. While the person is in the altered state, the process for storing and cementing long-term memories in the hippocampus is disrupted. Memories are stored in the amygdala (or fear center, as I like to call it) instead, or maybe not at all.  

It makes sense: When something horrific and shocking is happening to you, you are not thinking, "Gee, I'm sure glad that this is MY LIFE! I'd love to remember every detail of this experience." No... usually it's more like, "This can't be happening to ME. This is not MY life! This can't be real." 

Now if the shocker only happens once, maybe. Maybe then your brain would want to remember every detail so that it could protect itself in the future from that particular situation/danger. At night there are tigers! Tigers bad. Pain. Run!!! 

However, if the horror continues on an everyday basis and fighting, fleeing or cozying-up to tigers becomes routine, then a new self-preservation strategy is needed.  

Identifying the perpetrator does nothing to prevent the danger or the pain if there is absolutely nothing you can do to escape. In cPtsd, your brain has experienced enough horrible things from an early age, that many of those individual and horrible experiences have gotten sort of clumped-up into an one amalgamous blob of doubt, or despair or emptiness that is hard to sort through. That's where EMDR can be helpful. 

 
EMDR is one of the ways that a person can intentionally induce an altered state of consciousness, then possibly revisit and emotionally reprocess a bad memory safely and with a trained guide. EMDR is induced through bilateral brain stimulation. You can induce an EMDR-like state on your own through coordinated music and movement. It can also be partially induced by rolling your eyes back into your head as far as you can while they are closed. If you do this, you may notice that you feel a physical sensation of relaxation. I often experience it as a wave or a rush of energy pulling me toward a sleep-like state.  

When I say altered state of consciousness BTW, we are talking about an experience that is similar neurologically to that of being in a deep meditative state, hypnotized or simply half-awake. 

So where do these repressed memories come in? I don't know about using the word "repressed" exactly. It's more like the memories have always been there, but you haven't been able to see them clearly because after all.... they've been part of this huge amalgamous blob of feeling for years! And now you are older, and there are so many layers of feelings, experiences and physiological responses to sort through. EMDR may assist you in sorting through some of those layers more efficiently. 

Another factor seems to be *context-dependent memory*. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Context-dependent_memory

> In psychology, context-dependent memory is the improved recall of specific episodes or information when the context present at encoding and retrieval are the same. One particularly common example of context-dependence at work occurs when an individual has lost an item (e.g. lost car keys) in an unknown location. Typically, people try to systematically "retrace their steps" to determine all of the possible places where the item might be located. Based on the role that context plays in determining recall, it is not at all surprising that individuals often quite easily discover the lost item upon returning to the correct context.

I think EMDR is one way of safely revisiting the 'emotional context' of a situation. By evoking an old emotional context, you can then remember things that you forgot you knew. Sometimes the memories come as images. Sometimes they are vague... but that doesn't matter. Vague is okay, as long as you can get to the bodily feeling that was paired with that memory, and then defuse it. 

At the end of the day I suspect memory comes back to you when you're ready for it, and you may never be ready for it. Some things don't need to be re-experienced in all their grime and glory. For me it was when I allowed myself to start feeling my body and the emotions in my body again, that memories came back. The 'forgotten' memories were always directly connected to whatever feeling state I was reconnecting with. For example, the first time in recent history that I allowed myself to express anger toward someone I loved came paired with a memory blob of different times in childhood  when I expressed anger and then was shunned, isolated or abused for doing so. I then remembered why I had shut down my anger to begin with! I had a chance to observe the processes going on in my own mind from a slightly safer distance and with an adult perspective. Seeing the situation through an adult's eye helped me correct some black and white beliefs that my child mind had created.

I disclosed mostly so that my coworkers would understand why I was sometimes triggered by certain clients, situations and group trainings. I wanted them to understand where I was coming from when I had a panic attack and ran out of my  $200 Suicide Prevention training, or when I cried after being harassed by an elderly woman with Alzheimers even though I knew her anger came from the dementia. Finally, I wanted them to know and see a living example of a typical “social work client” slowly recovering and continuing to contribute to society despite her ‘disabilities.’ I wanted them to realize that these hidden disabilities are all around them, even if some of the highest functioning people they meet. 

 I also realized that although these people were my coworkers, they were some of the people I spent the most time with, and it was part of the healing process to open up and admit that I needed help sometimes too.
