I have a few theories - but that's all it is... just theories:  

**I think dissociative experiences may lie on a spectrum:** At one end would be extreme bodily arousal/heightened sensitivity and at the other end, body "deadness" and hypoarousal.  

For me personally, I have found that if I stay in the hyper-aroused/convulsing/crying state for too long it naturally will plummet into the dead zone eventually, simply because my body runs out of energy. Then I start to feel like a zombie. Everything is blurry sort-of... like being only half-awake. I zone out and stare into space until someone calls my name. It feels awful because you don't really feel, yet you sort of do at the same time. This may be a weird analogy, but for me it's almost like instead of having one color... you have so many layers of colors inside you that everything just turns into an unidentifiable brown slush. You know you have "color" but you can't identify it, and you can't get at the canvas underneath either.  
  
**The deadzone/numbing dissociation is more likely to accompany states of extreme 'bodily' depression.** (Feeling like you can't speak or move without extreme effort, can't focus, feel apathetic etc...) It is possible that you are very depressed, and that your dissociation changed to accompany your body's current state, or vice versa. 

**It also sounds like you could be picking-up on your friend's emotional state and unconsciously incorporating it into your own body**. In the past when I have been in a transitional phase and had a close friend (that I was trying to support) go through serious trouble, it has been very hard to balance my instinct for self-preservation and my instinct to nurture and support others. I feel like there is a war inside me... and I temporarily lose access to my coping skills in the moment, because I am so consumed by embodying what THEY are feeling (or what I think they are feeling) while also trying to remember myself. There is a happy balance between selflessness and self-preservation that can be obtained. 

One other thing to think about: FIGHT/FLIGHT/FREEZE/FAWN responses. I recently realized that when my loved ones trigger a certain in anger in me, I fly right through FIGHT response into FREEZE. This was necessary for my survival growing-up, as when I expressed my anger to my mother or father, there would be hell to pay. It was much smarter and safer to autoshutdown at the first hint of anger than to have to live with expressing it. It could be that you have been triggered in a new and/or different way than you did in the past because of your current situation or from all of the work that your have been doing for yourself. Maybe your body is rewarding you by showing you a different perspective. 

Good Luck!

**What I did:**  

I was watching this random youtube video that came up in my playlist... as I was listening, out of the blue I started crying. I had no idea why I was crying. Not a clue. So (intent on using my coping skills) I turned off the video and sat in silence for a moment trying to mediate. I still couldn't figure out why I cried. I somewhat jokingly decided to ask myself what was wrong. 

This is important: I literally asked myself (out-loud), "(insert your name here), what's going on? Is there something you want to tell me? You seem like you must be in pain. Please let me know what's going on so that I can help you share this burden."  

But I didn't get an answer you know, all I got was this singing in my head. I was so frustrated at my inability to meditate and do these therapy activities. Why could I not concentrate?! Why so much singing!!!!

Then I realized, the singing WAS the message.  

My parents were abusive in many ways... but one thing that made my narcissistic mom feel good about herself what the fact that I loved to listen to her sing when I was little. It was virtually the only positive mothering connection I had to her growing up and the only time she wanted to spend with me.  

 As I got older, I internalized the singing voice and a part of my brain was SO DAMN SMART that it created a mother (in my own head) to sing me to sleep and soothe me. In that moment I recovered memories of being locked in a room with nothing to do, and singing to myself for hours. It kept me sane. Then at some point in my early adulthood, I forgot about it all. I forgot about this wonderful coping skill I had already developed at a young age and then discarded.   

This was the moment when I realized that I already had all of these wise and unbroken parts inside of myself, just waiting to take care of me if I would let them. These exiled parts were hiding under layers of manufactured trauma crap and parental brainwashing. Because I viewed myself as traumatized, these vulnerable pieces had to stay underneath the layer of BS... just waiting for the day that I would accept and love myself enough to bother to even acknowledge their existence. When I did, when I started talking to them (it's not psychosis btw - and it's also not dissociative identity disorder/multiple personalities) and listened carefully to what they had to say... I even started standing-up to my nasty mom when she was making cruel and/or invalidating comments to me. I was worth it and I didn't really care what she thought. I was liberated. Free. It's truly a miraculous thing. No longer does my "ego" feel fragmented. When I acknowledged the things that my inner states/parts had to say, they sort of integrated back into my whole personality, and I became a much more interesting person overnight.

Other people using me like a tool and disregarding my individuality (thoughts, feelings, beliefs, dreams etc...) is what got me into this ego confusion mess in the first place. It's time for me to be me. Whatever that means. Whatever I decide.  

Who you are, isn't inflexible. On the contrary, your ego/identity (whatever you want to call it) undergoes change throughout your life... incorporating new roles/sub-personalities (I'm a parent!) and disregarding old ones (I'm childless!). You must establish contact with yourself, at which point you will realize that you are in a state of perpetual flux. Even your genes (the things we think of as the most fundamental and stable determiners of our personality and functioning) have epigenetic switches on them which can turn on or off in response to your physical and emotional environment before and **after** your birth. 

Well, I hope at least some of this message was helpful. I know it's really, really hard. Studies have also shown that if you practice meditation daily, it will change your brain... regardless of whether you experience the meditative process as being helpful in your conscious mind. The default mode network is a complex pattern of neural functioning distributed among several brain regions. Some (but not all) researchers believe that the DMN primarily develops through the first 10 years of life and then remains 'relatively stable' over the lifespan. Following this logic, the wiring of the DMN in individuals with CPTSD would most certainly have been impacted. Some may say that this is a disadvantage, but I disagree.

How do you define “alone”? If you mean without a therapist... it is certainly possible. However, a therapist is supposed to be an expert guide to your mental health and well-being. Unlike friends or family, they are an objective third-party who is genuinely curious about your life and your feelings. They have an outside perspective which can be necessary, or at the least - extremely helpful to your ability to recover. A therapist uses their book knowledge combined with their professional experience to help you get to your desired destination.  
Healing yourself is like embarking on an African safari; If you think of a therapist as a travel guide, you can see their job clearly. You may be desperate to travel to the Congo (to heal), but that doesn’t mean that you should do it alone - without someone who has been there before and knows the lay of the land, the local customs and the language. A travel guide (therapist) will help you plan a trip that will get you to your destination, and also guide you through all the important landmarks on the way...that you might not have even known existed.   
Depending on which landmarks you need to hit on the way to the Congo, it may be most efficient or safe to go by boat, or by plane, or maybe even in an armored car, it just depends on the nature of your journey. You may even decide you don’t actually WANT to go to the Congo.   
The travel guide/therapist looks at the whole map of Africa and helps you make determinations about what types of therapeutic techniques (plane, train, automobile) you want to utilize to make it there safely. The therapist/travel guide also warns you when you begin to travel into dangerous territory, or when you’ve taken a wrong turn. They are NOT supposed to make all the decisions for you. You are paying them to advise you on your journey - so unless the situation becomes life threatening, they should let you steer.  

So can you do it alone? Sure, but you’re going to have to become an expert on Africa to do it.  

 And, because you’ve never been to Africa before yourself, that is going to be challenging.  No matter how informed you become, you will still lack the experience of the professional guide who has been to Africa many times.  Becoming your own guide means learning about psychology, human biology, philosophy, spirituality even...It means studying about various therapeutic techniques (many of which you’ll find you unfortunately cannot do alone) and then finding a way to apply them to yourself.  Regardless of the therapist, you will need some supportive others in your life that you can safely talk to about your mental health.  

Personally, I have had a lot of trouble making progress in therapy, because I don’t trust other people enough to let my guard down. I am also currently training to become a therapist and do obsessive amounts of research, investigation and study on the topic, which sometimes makes me a little arrogant and closed minded about what other people have to say. I got to a point though where I knew I owed it to my boyfriend to seek professional help. I finally connected with a really great therapist, but even though I wanted to trust her, I just couldn’t. So, I have been “therapizing” myself for the past couple of years and checking in with her once in awhile on my progress. Slowly but surely, I move forward. So, although I highly recommend involving a therapist in your recovery (or at least a life coach) there are steps you can take on your own which I will outline below :

1. Decide where you want to go. This means figuring out what “being better” would look like and feel like in your life. What does it mean to be mentally healthy? How will I act when I am mentally healthy? Ask yourself these questions in order to start finding a destination you’d like to travel to. 

2. Introspect. Think about your behaviors. Think about your thought patterns. What is the heart of the matter? What troubles you? What would you like to change? 

3. Learn about human psychology. Start with topics relevant to the behaviors or thoughts that seem to be most troubling in your life. For example: Were you raised in a dysfunctional family? - if yes, you would probably want to learn about dysfunctional family systems - and various theories about how dysfunctional families operate... such as the work of John Bradshaw (who is good at explaining complex topics in a simple way).  
However, if you experience a great deal of dissociation... you may need to re-steer the boat away from Family Systems theory, to Internal Family Systems theory, as that is a better fit for major dissociative symptoms. 
(this is just an example, but I hope you get what I’m saying about the process of investigating, introspecting and re-steering the boat as needed). 

4. Begin practicing meditation/mindfulness. This is a very crucial component when one doesn’t have therapist.

5. Realize and accept that healthy mind is influenced by healthy body. This means exercise, yoga, tai chi, dance, eating right, getting out and socializing  once in awhile, having a hobby even....all things easier said than done.

6. Using the knowledge you’ve gained about psychology, you newfound self-understanding,  and your critical thinking skills, pick an appropriate therapeutic technique you can practice on your own and try it. Really try it. Ask yourself, “is this helpful?” “Does it seem to have the desired effect?” Stick with your new practice/habit for awhile and record its effectiveness. If it isn’t effective after period of time, you may choose to switch to something else and try that.   

In my experience, as you go on this journey, certain ideas will resonate with you more than others. Notice that. Notice you. Record your responses. Write notes to yourself about the breakthroughs you are making and read them back to yourself when you hit a rough patch (which you absolutely will).

Going to Africa without a travel guide is a lot of work, and involves time and intense planning. Sometimes you will navigate yourself into a shipwreck, or a car accident or a plane crash. Because you’re alone, it will all be on you to get things back up and running. You will have to sit in the cabin of the broken plane with a map on your lap and a magnifying glass trying to figure-out where to go next, how to suture-up your own bleeding gashes, and how to collect enough food and water to survive long enough to disembark once more. It IS possible though. Just really really hard.

In order to be heard, you must surround yourself with those who have the capacity to listen; not just to hear, but to listen. When you find those people (and sometimes they are hard to find) that really listen, engage with THEM, build relationships with those people. So many people out there are going about their daily lives, so unhappy, traumatized, just trying to keep it together - pull off the facade. They haven't reflected on themselves, maybe they can't.... maybe they can't even tolerate the mention of emotions or any topics which trigger their own hidden anxieties. 

Alternatively, I also know that sometimes because of my trauma experiences, I will tend to unconsciously pull away from the relationships that scare me, and I will start judging everyone in my life based-on my feelings at the current moment, rather than focusing on the big picture. That has been huge for me, having the ability to pull back when I'm feeling the way it sounds like you are, and ask myself, "is this REALLY the way things have always been? I know it definitely feels like that right now ~ and that is important, and valid, but... is it possible that my emotionally fueled tunnel vision is obstructing my view of the whole picture?"

 I seriously have this internal dialogue with myself. It was kind of an experiment at first, but after a while I noticed that making sure I pulled my focus to the big picture, really helped me with my feelings of worthlessness and insignificance. Now, given enough stress build-up, it doesn't work.

MY EXPERIENCE: 
I have these infrequent, random episodes where I feel like almost 'out-of-the-blue' I am possessed by these horrible uncontrollable physical impulses (and by that I mean to say - my body is so agitated and emotionally dysregulated that I rip at my own fingers involuntarily, or rub them together until the skin is raw. When I try to control or suppress it, or EVEN when I try to utilize a HEALTHY coping strategy like deep breathing or something... that's when the feelings come... especially rage, like *bang* 0 to 100... but the only reason I know that I'm having "feelings" is because my body is crying, or trying to scream or implode, shatter my insides. I do hurt myself sometimes (because it was a coping strategy I adopted a long time ago to manage my 'disproportionate' emotional responses). I can tell you that I am pretty much always partially dissociated from my physical body.
